items.title: « Escroc », la nouvelle perfusion musicale de Grand Docteur
items.description: Le reggaeman burkinabè Grand Docteur a accordé une interview à Faso7 le 22 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou pour défendre son nouveau clip intitulé « Escroc ». Dans ce titre chanté en mooré, l'artiste dit s'attaquer à la prolifération de personnes qui « apparaissent » et se présentent comme des guérisseurs, des fetichistes, des pasteurs ou des hadja dotés de pouvoirs divins et dont il doute de la probité de certains. Grand Docteur dit d’emblée que son ancêtre Naaba Baongho était féticheur, son grand-père Naaba Na Waam Taõré était féticheur, son père Kouma aussi. Il se revendique lui-même « traditionnaliste pur » . C'est précisément ce bagage qui lui donne, selon lui, la légitimité pour dénoncer. « Je connais ce que ça veut dire, soigner quelqu'un, aider quelqu'un dans la tradition. Et tous ceux qui viennent en disant que Dieu leur a donné le savoir pour soulager la population. Ils n'ont pas payé. C'est ce qu'ils disent. Mais si à un moment donné, ce que Dieu t'a donné gratuitement, pour te voir maintenant, il y a du privé alors que tu ne l'as pas vu en privé pour prendre… Il y a quelque chose qui cloche quelque part » , a-t-il expliqué. Le titre ne vise pas la tradition ni les religions dans leur ensemble, dit-il. Grand Docteur l'a précisé lui-même, en soulignant qu'il s'attaque aux mauvaises graines, pas à ceux qui ont fait leur preuves. « Même chez nous les artistes, il y a des faux artistes. (…). Voilà pourquoi j'interpelle toute la population à la vigilance et à la méfiance » , a-t-il indiqué. Il illustre son propos par le témoignage d'une proche dont la mère malade a refusé les soins médicaux après avoir entendu des témoignages à la radio sur une guérisseuse. La fille a contracté un crédit pour financer cette alternative. La mère marche aujourd'hui avec des béquilles. « Mon rôle, c'est de diagnostiquer, de conscientiser, de prévenir. Depuis des années, je suis dans ça. Chaque mal qui vient, je diagnostique et puis je passe un morceau » , a-t-il dit. De Petit à Grand Docteur : une histoire de survie En marge du sujet principal, Grand Docteur a raconté l'origine de son nom, devenu Grand Docteur après des années passées sous l'appellation Petit Docteur. L'histoire remonte à 1993, quand il arrive à Ouagadougou, travaille comme employé de maison, fabrique des briques en banco, puis pousse une barrique à eau pendant trois ans. Un malaise dans la cour d'un client l'envoie à l'hôpital Yalgado. Il en ressort avec 1 200 francs CFA, toutes ses économies de trois ans dilapidées en ordonnances. Il achète des médicaments de la rue au marché et se lance dans leur revente. Un vendeur plus grand que lui dormait avec lui sur le même trottoir. Pour les distinguer, l'un devient Grand Docteur, l'autre Petit Docteur. Le surnom traverse la photographie, la vente de cassettes, la réparation de téléphones portables, jusqu'à la musique. Le changement de nom est venu d'une leçon reçue en Côte d'Ivoire lors d'un concours où il représentait le Burkina Faso. Des anciens de la musique africaine l'avaient pris à part pour lui citer des artistes dont le nom contenait le mot « Petit » : tous disparus malgré leur talent. « Tu ne peux pas dépasser ton nom. Les conditions vont te faire rester petit » , lui avaient-ils dit. Il a annoncé le changement sur sa page. Pas sans craindre les réactions. « Je connais l'esprit burkinabè. Ils ne vont jamais venir te demander pourquoi ton nom est Grand Docteur. Ils vont juste dire que tu te gonfles. Mais j'étais obligé » , a-t-il confié. Sa carrière, dit-il, se porte bien. Il vit de la musique, il joue dans des villes où il ne pouvait pas aller il y a encore quelques années, grâce aux succès des opérations de reconquête du territoire national. Grand Docteur prépare déjà son prochain titre, qu'il intitulera « Incompris » . Un autoportrait, sans doute. Josué TIENDREBEOGO Faso7 L’article « Escroc », la nouvelle perfusion musicale de Grand Docteur est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Oti Akenteng slams GFA for ‘disrespect’ of local coaches in national team appointments
items.description: Former Technical Director of the Ghana Football Association (GFA), Francis Oti Akenteng, has questioned the role of the institution in ignoring local coaches during national team appointments. Akenteng’s statement follows Kim Lars Björkegren’s appointment as the interim technical team lead for the Black Stars ahead of the doubleheader against Somalia in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifiers. The Black Stars have lost their opening two matches in the qualifiers following a 2-0 defeat to Ivory Coast in Bouaké and a humiliating 4-2 loss to Gambia at the Accra Sports Stadium. The results led to former Portuguese head coach Carlos Queiroz and the GFA mutually parting ways. Bjorkegren will be assisted by Medeama head coach Ibrahim Tanko and Godwin Attram, with Fatawu Dauda still remaining the goalkeeper coach. Akenteng admitted that Ghana has many experienced local coaches, and when given the privilege, could coach the Black Stars on an interim basis. “There are local coaches who are capable of coaching the Black Stars,” he said in an interview with Asempa FM. “If they are always overlooked, that is a sign of disrespect, and if the local coaches are not respected, they will not have an interest in coaching.” Black Stars remain at the bottom of Group C and are set to face Somalia in November, after which Bjorkegren will turn attention to the Black Queens, who fight for a spot in the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup with the play-off preliminary phase scheduled between November 24 and December 5, 2026.

items.title: Agroalimentaire : le groupe qatari Baladna examine un projet d’investissement dans la production de lait en poudre
items.description: Le geant qatari de l'agroalimentaire Baladna prepare un nouveau projet d'investissement en Algerie. Son premier projet dans le pays, « emblematique » de la cooperation algero-qatarie, a abouti au lancement d'une immense ferme devant compter 270 000 vaches laitieres, en cours de realisation dans la wilaya d'Adrar, a 1 400 km au sud-ouest d'Alger, pour un investissement de 3,5 milliards de dollars. Le nouveau projet a ete evoque le 25 octobre par le directeur general de l'Agence algerienne de promotion de l'investissement Omar Rekkache, qui a fait savoir que Baladna « examine actuellement un autre projet, dont les preparatifs sont en cours », sans apporter de plus amples details. Les propos ont ete tenus en marge de la 9e edition du Forum mondial de l'investissement, organisee a Doha par l'etat du Qatar et la Conference des Nations unies sur le commerce et le developpement, sous le theme « Investir dans l'avenir ». Appel a « explorer les opportunites prometteuses offertes par l'Algerie » Dans ses declarations a l'Agence de presse du Qatar, Omar Rekkache a mis en avant les opportunites d'investissement entre l'Algerie et le Qatar, soulignant la volonte commune d'elargir leur cooperation et de lui ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives. Dans ce contexte, il a appele les investisseurs qataris a « tirer parti de ses atouts economiques et a envisager le lancement de nouveaux projets de nature a renforcer le partenariat economique entre les deux pays, au service de leurs interets communs et du developpement de leurs relations bilaterales ». Les investissements du Qatar en Algerie ne se limitent pas a l'agroalimentaire ; la cooperation economique entre les deux pays comprend, en effet, la creation de la societe Algerian Qatari Steel , specialisee dans la siderurgie, et la presence de l'operateur Ooredoo Algerie, actif dans les telecommunications. Le projet de la ferme geante d'Adrar vise a produire, a lui seul, 1,7 milliard de litres de lait cru par an, qui serviront a fabriquer 193 000 tonnes de poudre de lait, avec pour objectif de couvrir 50 % des besoins nationaux des 2028. L'Algerie espere ainsi reduire de 1,5 milliard de dollars la facture de ses importations, renforcer sa souverainete alimentaire et faire du Sahara « un pole d'excellence agricole », selon la presse locale.

items.title: 24 morts dans une collision entre un bus et un camion
items.description: Au moins 24 personnes ont péri et une vingtaine d’autres ont été blessées dans une collision entre un bus et un camion survenue, le dimanche 25 octobre 2026, sur l’autoroute reliant Nairobi à Mombasa, selon la police kényane. Ce drame relance l’alerte sur l’insécurité routière au Kenya, où plus de 5 000 personnes meurent chaque année sur les routes, selon les chiffres avancés par l’Autorité nationale de sécurité des transports. Le Kenya est une nouvelle fois frappé par un drame routier meurtrier. Dimanche 25 octobre 2026, au moins 24 personnes ont perdu la vie dans une violente collision entre un bus et un camion sur l’axe Nairobi-Mombasa, l’une des principales voies de circulation du pays. Le bilan fait, également, état d'une vingtaine de blessés. Plusieurs victimes ont été prises en charge à l’hôpital de Mtito Andei, a indiqué son directeur médical, Paul Kisienya, cité par des médias. Selon les informations rapportées, les passagers du bus rentraient à Mombasa après avoir assisté aux funérailles de leur pasteur dans l’ouest du pays. Les circonstances exactes de la collision restent à déterminer. Un axe routier endeuillé à répétition Ce nouvel accident ravive les inquiétudes autour de la sécurité sur l’autoroute Nairobi-Mombasa. En l’espace de trois semaines, cet axe a été le théâtre de deux accidents meurtriers, le précédent ayant fait 17 morts. Face à cette succession de tragédies, l’Autorité nationale de sécurité des transports réclame que ces accidents soient déclarés catastrophe nationale. L’organisme alerte sur l’ampleur du phénomène, avec environ 20 000 accidents et plus de 5 000 morts recensés chaque année au Kenya. Ruto ordonne l’inspection des véhicules de transport public Au lendemain de ce nouveau drame, le président kényan William Ruto a présenté ses condoléances aux familles endeuillées et ordonné l’inspection de tous les véhicules de transport public. Il a également exhorté les conducteurs à respecter le code de la route. La répétition de ces accidents pose une nouvelle fois la question de l’efficacité des mesures de prévention et du renforcement des contrôles sur les routes du pays. Au-delà du lourd bilan humain de cette collision, l’urgence demeure: éviter que les routes kényanes ne continuent de se transformer en pièges mortels pour leurs usagers. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article 24 morts dans une collision entre un bus et un camion est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: 2e édition de la SNLCC : une journée portes ouvertes à la BCLCC pour sensibiliser sur la cybercriminalité
items.description: Dans le cadre de la 2e édition de la Semaine nationale de lutte contre la cybercriminalité (SNLCC), la Brigade centrale de lutte contre la cybercriminalité (BCLCC) a organisé une journée portes ouvertes (JPO), ce 26 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou. Il s'agit de rapprocher l'institution du grand public afin de le sensibiliser et de prévenir certaines infractions. Cette année, la Semaine nationale de lutte contre la cybercriminalité (SNLCC) se tient sous le thème : « Cybercriminalité et menaces numériques émergentes : du clic au crime ». Elle traduit la nécessité de sensibiliser les populations aux infractions commises sur les réseaux sociaux. Selon le Commandant Ahmed Ouédraogo, secrétaire général du ministère de la Sécurité, cette thématique a été retenue, car la majorité des utilisateurs des plateformes numériques ignorent les réglementations en vigueur, d'où la survenue de certains écarts de comportement. Il a cependant invité les populations à se rendre dans les locaux de la BCLCC afin de s'imprégner des différentes mesures. Les acteurs de la JPO de la BCLCC©️Faso7 « C'est une opportunité qui est offerte à la population de pouvoir se rapprocher des différents acteurs pour mieux être informé, c'est-à-dire avoir toutes les informations nécessaires sur comment utiliser les réseaux sociaux et éviter, en tout cas, de se faire prendre, on va dire, par des écarts de comportement», a-t-il indiqué. Le commissaire principal de Police Akim Nignan, commandant de la BCLCC, a ajouté que cette semaine sera marquée par des sensibilisations à travers une caravane, des panels et un maracana des acteurs. Également, il sera organisé un hackathon au profit des jeunes afin de leur permettre de mettre leur savoir-faire au service de la lutte contre la cybercriminalité. Le commandant de la BCLCC a rappelé que l'objectif est de sensibiliser et de prévenir des cas d'infractions qui ont été commis auparavant. Il est aussi question de fédérer les actions des différents acteurs pour venir à bout de la cybercriminalité. « Nous savions bien que nos populations écoutent et pour cela, nous savions que la sensibilisation qui sera faite va porter donc fruits et nous aurons moins affaire à des populations qui posent des actes malveillants sur les réseaux sociaux » , a expliqué le commissaire principal de Police Akim Nignan. Les JPO de la BCLCC ont réuni différents acteurs, dont l'ARCOD, la Brigade Laabal et l'Office national d'identification. La 2e édition de la SNLCC se déroule du 26 au 30 octobre 2026. Cheick Habib Désiré BAYILI Faso7 L’article 2e édition de la SNLCC : une journée portes ouvertes à la BCLCC pour sensibiliser sur la cybercriminalité est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Former army chief Abdul Waheed Kakar passes away in Rawalpindi
items.description: Former army chief Abdul Waheed Kakar passed away in Rawalpindi on Monday, a statement by the military’s media affairs wing said. Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and all ranks of the Pakistan Army “express deep sorrow” over his demise, the statement by the Inter-Services Public Relations added. “The CDF and all ranks of the Pakistan Army pay tribute to the late general’s distinguished military career, leadership and invaluable services to the Pakistan Army. “Pakistan Army shares the grief of the bereaved family and offers its heartfelt condolences. May Allah Almighty grant the departed soul highest place in jannah and give the family strength and patience,” the statement said. The late general had served as Pakistan’s army chief from January 1993 to January 1996. He pressured then-president Ghulam Ishaq Khan and then-prime minister Nawaz Sharif to hand in their resignations, precipitating the 1993 elections in which Benazir Bhutto was elected as the prime minister. He had retired at the end of his term. President Asif Ali Zardari also expressed sorrow at the passing of the former army chief, conveying condolences to his family, according to a statement from his office. “The president prays for the bereaved family to be granted the strength to bear this loss with patience,” the statement read. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, expressing condolences at the death of the former general, paid tribute to his “invaluable services” to the Pakistan Armed Forces, state broadcaster PTV r eported. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, in a post on X, said he was “deeply saddened” by Kakar’s passing. “His distinguished service to Pakistan and the Pakistan Army will be remembered with the highest regard,” Dar wrote, praying for the deceased’s family. PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, in a statement on X, lauded the late general’s services to the nation as well as his “professional dedication and the manner in which he fulfilled his national duties”. Gohar added that Kakar will “always be remembered with honour and respect”.

items.title: Energies renouvelables: jusqu’à 25 milliards d’euros d'investissements mobilisés par l'UE
items.description: La Commission européenne entend mobiliser jusqu’à 25 milliards d’euros d'investissements d’ici 2035 pour des projets d’énergies renouvelables et de technologies propres dans la région méditerranéenne, à travers une plateforme d’investissement lancée lundi. La plateforme T-MED facilitera les investissements dans la production d’énergie renouvelable, les réseaux électriques, les interconnexions et les technologies propres, tout en assurant la formation et le renforcement des compétences de près de 10.000 travailleurs, indique l’Exécutif européen dans un communiqué. Cette plateforme constitue un élément clé de l’Initiative de coopération trans-méditerranéenne pour les énergies renouvelables et les technologies propres (T-MED), une initiative phare du Pacte pour la Méditerranée, relève la même source. Cette initiative a été présentée à Bruxelles par la commissaire européenne chargée de la Méditerranée, Dubravka Šuica, lors d’un événement réunissant des institutions financières européennes et internationales, des investisseurs privés et des promoteurs de projets, afin d’identifier des opportunités d’investissement et des projets susceptibles de bénéficier du soutien de la Commission. Ce soutien prendra la forme de garanties pouvant atteindre 4,5 milliards d’euros, mobilisées dans le cadre du Fonds européen pour le développement durable Plus (FEDD+), affirme Bruxelles, notant que ces garanties permettront de réduire les risques liés aux investissements, d’attirer des capitaux privés et d’accélérer la mise en œuvre de projets viables dans le domaine des énergies renouvelables et des technologies propres dans toute la région. La plateforme facilitera la coopération entre les institutions financières, les investisseurs et les promoteurs de projets, en mettant en relation des projets prometteurs avec des sources de financement potentielles et en aidant à transformer des opportunités d’investissement en projets concrets, poursuit le communiqué. “La région méditerranéenne recèle un potentiel considérable, encore inexploité, en matière d’énergies renouvelables”, estime la Commission, ajoutant que la plateforme T-MED vise à libérer ce potentiel en soutenant des investissements dans la production d’électricité renouvelable, l’hydrogène renouvelable, les réseaux de transport et de distribution d’électricité, le stockage de l’énergie, les interconnexions transfrontalières et la fabrication de technologies propres. Au-delà du financement, la plateforme soutiendra les efforts visant à améliorer les cadres réglementaires, les procédures d’autorisation, l’accès au réseau et les contrats d’achat d’électricité, tout en favorisant le développement des compétences et des chaînes de valeur locales dans le secteur des technologies propres. “En levant ces obstacles à l’investissement, T-MED contribuera à renforcer la sécurité énergétique, à approfondir la coopération économique et à créer de nouvelles opportunités de croissance durable dans toute la Méditerranée”, assure la Commission. items.title: Ondo Assembly passes bill for establishment of state police
items.description: Ondo State House of Assembly has passed a bill seeking to amend the 1999 Constitution to provide for the establishment of state police services. The bill was passed following deliberations by the lawmakers at a plenary session on Monday in Akure. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the proposal was conveyed to the assembly in a letter from the National Assembly Clerk, Kamoru Ogunlana, which was read by the Speaker, Olamide Oladiji, on Sept. 24. The House Leader, Olatunji Oshati, who moved for the passage and its transmission to the National Assembly, said the lawmakers had considered the implications of the proposed amendment for the citizenry. Oshati said that the establishment of state police would address the numerous security challenges confronting the country. The motion was seconded by Mr Allen Oluwatoyin, All Progressives Congress (APC), member representing Ese-Odo State Constituency. Also speaking, Oladiji described the proposed establishment of state police as long overdue, saying it would enable security agencies to respond more swiftly to crime and other security concerns. He noted that state policing, being grassroots-based, would reduce crime through improved intelligence gathering and proactive security measures. “There will be greater confidence in state policing. It will strengthen intelligence gathering and provide grassroots security,” he added. The speaker, however, commended the lawmakers for their contributions to the bill and its passage. It was gathered that the bill would be transmitted to the National Assembly for further legislative consideration. items.title: Filière avicole : Le Burkina Faso lance la formation de 1 000 acteurs
items.description: Le gouvernement burkinabè a lancé, le 24 octobre 2026, à l’École nationale de formation agricole de Matourkou (ENAFA), une campagne de formation de 1 000 acteurs de la filière avicole, dont 763 bassecouriers et 237 gestionnaires de fermes. Inscrite dans le cadre de l’Offensive agropastorale, hydraulique et halieutique 2026-2028, cette initiative vise à renforcer les capacités des acteurs pour accroître la production nationale de poulets de chair, de poussins et d’œufs à couver. À travers ce programme, les autorités ambitionnent de contribuer à la souveraineté alimentaire du Burkina Faso, notamment en réduisant la dépendance du pays aux importations de produits avicoles. Cette vision, portée par le Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, repose entre autres sur le renforcement des compétences techniques et managériales des acteurs de première ligne du secteur de l’élevage. Le Dr Amadou Dicko, ministre délégué chargé des Ressources animales, représentant le ministre d’État, le Commandant Ismaël Sombié, ministre de l’Agriculture, a mis l’accent sur la nécessité de doter les producteurs et les gestionnaires de fermes des connaissances nécessaires pour améliorer durablement les performances de la filière. Le gouvernement a ainsi initié « ce programme ambitieux » afin de renforcer les capacités de 1 000 bénéficiaires issus de différentes localités du pays. Prévue sur une durée de 30 jours, la formation accorde une place importante aux exercices pratiques. Selon le Dr Amadou Dicko, ce calendrier permettra aux apprenants de suivre les différentes étapes de l’élevage d’une bande de volailles, de la réception des poussins jusqu’à l’abattage. L’organisation du programme tient également compte des contraintes et des occupations des participants. Au-delà des apprentissages techniques liés à la conduite des élevages, le programme comprend des modules consacrés au civisme, au patriotisme et aux valeurs morales. Cette approche vise à associer le renforcement des compétences professionnelles à la promotion de valeurs jugées essentielles à l’engagement des acteurs dans le développement national. Renforcer son potentiel de production avicole S’adressant aux 763 bassecouriers et aux 237 gestionnaires de fermes, le ministre délégué a insisté sur les responsabilités spécifiques de chaque catégorie dans le développement de la filière. Pour les bassecouriers, l’accent sera mis sur la maîtrise des techniques de biosécurité, l’alimentation des volailles et le suivi sanitaire. Ces compétences sont essentielles pour limiter les risques de maladies, réduire les pertes et améliorer les conditions d’élevage. Les gestionnaires de fermes, quant à eux, seront outillés pour renforcer leurs capacités en matière de gestion technique, financière et logistique. La maîtrise de ces différents aspects constitue un levier important pour améliorer la rentabilité des exploitations et assurer leur viabilité économique. À travers cette formation différenciée, le gouvernement entend agir à la fois sur les pratiques d’élevage et sur la gestion des unités de production. L’objectif est de disposer d’acteurs mieux préparés à répondre à la demande nationale en produits avicoles. Selon Émilien Bakoné, directeur général de la production animale, les participants proviennent de divers horizons du Burkina Faso. Leur sélection a été effectuée sur la base de critères objectifs définis par un comité national. Au total, 2 000 candidatures ont été enregistrées pour cette campagne, témoignant de l’intérêt suscité par cette initiative auprès des acteurs de la filière. Avec la formation de ces 1 000 bénéficiaires, le Burkina Faso entend renforcer son potentiel de production avicole. Cette action s’inscrit dans une stratégie plus large visant à couvrir les besoins nationaux en poulets de chair, en poussins et en œufs à couver, tout en consolidant les bases d’une filière avicole plus performante et moins dépendante de l’extérieur. items.title: El real brasileño registra su peor sesión en más de tres décadas tras la inesperada victoria de Lula
items.description: La remontada de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva en las presidenciales brasileñas no solo ha sorprendido a las urnas. También ha obligado a los mercados a replantearse un escenario que daban por descontado y ha desencadenado una sacudida histórica. La Bolsa de São Paulo se ha visto obligada a activar el mecanismo de interrupción automática de la negociación tras desplomarse un 10%, un umbral que no alcanzaba desde el estallido de la pandemia en 2020. Horas antes, el operador bursátil había ampliado hasta el 20% el rango de oscilación permitido para absorber la volatilidad. Para encontrar un episodio de magnitud comparable hay que remontarse a 1992, cuando el mercado brasileño quedó atrapado por la crisis política que acabaría desembocando en la destitución del presidente Fernando Collor de Mello. Con la negociación suspendida en São Paulo, los inversores toman como referencia el ETF que replica la Bolsa brasileña y cotiza en Nueva York, que se deja un 24%. Por su parte, el índice de pequeñas empresas brasileñas se desploma un 30%, la mayor caída de su historia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: PLF 2027 : l’État réinscrit 6 milliards de DH de privatisations
items.description: Absente du projet de loi de finances 2026, la ligne consacrée aux produits de cession de participations de l’État fait son retour dans le PLF 2027, à hauteur de 6 milliards de dirhams, sans que le texte désigne la moindre cible. Le projet de loi de finances n° 60-26 pour 2027 remet à son tableau de recettes un poste que le texte précédent avait laissé vide : 6 milliards de dirhams attendus de la vente de participations publiques. Rangée à la nature de recette 60, dans la section dévolue à la Direction des entreprises publiques et de la privatisation, la ligne n’est assortie d’aucune précision sur les sociétés visées, sur l’échéancier ou sur la forme des opérations, qu’il s’agisse de privatisations proprement dites, d’ouvertures de capital ou de transferts entre entités publiques. Ce retour se comprend à la lumière des deux derniers exercices. La loi de finances 2025 avait tablé sur 9 milliards de dirhams au titre de ces opérations, répartis entre 6 milliards pour les privatisations et 3 milliards pour des ventes d’actifs ou des opérations entre organismes publics. Le volet des privatisations est pourtant resté lettre morte : aucune cession n’a été conclue au cours de l’année. Le PLF 2026 en avait tiré la conséquence en n’inscrivant aucun produit de cette nature, ce qui avait marqué une pause nette dans le programme. Le montant de 2027 correspond donc exactement à celui que la loi de finances 2025 réservait aux seules privatisations, sans la composante des cessions d’actifs. L’Exécutif rouvre ainsi une ligne qu’il avait fermée un an plus tôt, alors que le chantier juridique destiné à encadrer ces opérations n’est pas achevé. Cette réforme vise à moderniser les procédures de vente des participations publiques et à les rendre cohérentes avec la restructuration en cours des établissements et entreprises publics. À l’échelle du budget de l’État, la somme n’a rien d’anecdotique. Les recettes ordinaires du budget général sont évaluées à 482,4 milliards de dirhams, dont 437,4 milliards de recettes fiscales. Le solde du budget général, calculé hors produits des emprunts et hors amortissement de la dette, ressort à un déficit de 88,7 milliards, et les besoins bruts de financement de l’État atteignent 159,0 milliards. Les 6 milliards de cessions équivalent ainsi à près de 7 % de ce solde négatif. Ils se situent aussi dans le voisinage du dividende attendu de l’OCP, fixé à 6,4 milliards, et dépassent très largement les 995,2 millions de dirhams escomptés des participations financières de l’État dans diverses sociétés. Le projet ne dit rien des entités concernées, et ce silence n’a rien d’inédit. À la reprise du programme en 2019, le ministre des Finances d’alors avait déjà indiqué qu’aucune liste n’était arrêtée, en précisant seulement que les opérations porteraient sur des cessions ou des ouvertures de capital d’entités déjà constituées en sociétés anonymes. Sur le plan légal, la liste des entreprises et actifs privatisables comprend notamment Maroc Telecom, Marsa Maroc, l’hôtel La Mamounia, Énergie électrique de Tahaddart, Biopharma et la Société nationale de commercialisation de semences, Sonacos. Cette liste donne à l’État la faculté de lancer une vente lorsque la décision est prise, mais elle ne permet pas de savoir lesquelles de ces entités seront effectivement mises sur le marché en 2027. Un détail des annexes retient l’attention. Le service de l’État géré de manière autonome chargé de la privatisation figure dans les tableaux sans le moindre montant, ni en recettes ni en dépenses, que l’on considère l’exploitation ou l’investissement. L’enveloppe de 6 milliards repose donc sur une prévision de recettes du budget général, et non sur une dotation propre à ce service. La ligne s’inscrit enfin dans un ensemble de recettes non fiscales de nature patrimoniale, qui occupent une place significative dans l’équilibre du projet. Les produits à provenir de l’Agence nationale de la Conservation foncière, du Cadastre et de la Cartographie sont évalués à 7,2 milliards de dirhams, soit le montant le plus élevé parmi les établissements publics, tandis qu’une ligne de produits divers est fixée à 5 milliards de dirhams, sans le moindre détail. Avec les cessions de participations, ces trois lignes totalisent 18,2 milliards de dirhams de recettes dont le projet ne précise ni la mécanique ni les sources. The post PLF 2027 : l’État réinscrit 6 milliards de DH de privatisations appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: OmniBSIC Bank honoured with African Banking Excellence Award at IFAL 2026
items.description: OmniBSIC Bank Ghana Limited has been honoured with the African Banking Excellence Award for Growth, Innovation and Customer Value at the 12th International Forum on African-Caribbean Leadership (IFAL 2026), held in New York on the margins of the 81st United Nations General Assembly. The award recognises financial institutions across Africa that have demonstrated outstanding performance in driving growth, advancing innovation and delivering value to customers. OmniBSIC Bank’s recognition reflects its sustained transformation and growing position in Ghana’s financial services sector, supported by continued investment in technology, customer experience and strategic partnerships. The bank’s growth has been reflected in its recent financial performance. In 2025, OmniBSIC Bank more than doubled its total assets to GH¢21.58 billion, while customer deposits reached GH¢16.56 billion. Profit before tax also rose by 104 percent to GH¢641 million. Speaking on the recognition, Managing Director of OmniBSIC Bank, Daniel Asiedu, said the award was a significant affirmation of the bank’s ambition and its Ghanaian roots. “Receiving this award on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly is deeply meaningful to us. It affirms what we have always believed that a Ghanaian bank, built on local foundations and sustained by the trust of its customers, can compete and excel on the world stage. This is not merely a recognition of what we have achieved; it is a mandate for where we are going,” Mr. Asiedu said. The award comes as OmniBSIC Bank continues to implement its OmniBSIC 5.0 strategic initiative, which places technology-driven innovation, personalised service and proactive customer partnerships at the centre of its growth agenda. The bank has continued to expand its reach and deepen its engagement with individuals, small and medium-sized enterprises, corporates and institutions, while strengthening its digital banking capabilities and customer proposition. The IFAL honour adds to a strong record of local, international and pan-African recognition for OmniBSIC Bank and its leadership. The bank has been named Best Corporate Bank (Ghana) by Global Banking & Finance Review in 2023, 2024 and 2026, Fastest-Growing Corporate Bank (Ghana) in 2023, Bank of the Year at the Ghana Business Awards and Ghana Business Standard Awards in 2023 and 2024 respectively, and SME Bank of the Year at the Ghana Credit Excellence Awards in 2024. It has also been recognised twice as Most Customer-Centric Bank by CIMG and as Top Bank in Consumer Service Quality by the Ghana Customer Satisfaction Index in 2025. Daniel Asiedu receives honorary citizenship of Stonecrest In a further recognition of Ghanaian leadership and contribution to economic development, Mr. Asiedu was also conferred with Honorary Citizenship of the City of Stonecrest, Georgia, on the sidelines of IFAL 2026. The honour recognises his leadership and contribution to banking and economic development, as well as his commitment to advancing economic connections between Ghana, Africa and the global diaspora. Incorporated in 2016, Stonecrest is a municipality in DeKalb County, Georgia, with a focus on economic empowerment, inclusive development and international collaboration. Mr. Asiedu described the recognition as a personal honour and an opportunity to deepen his commitment to cross-border economic development. “I am deeply humbled by this honour from the City of Stonecrest. To be recognised by a city with such a purposeful and proud identity is an extraordinary privilege. It deepens my personal commitment to working across borders to advance economic development,” for Ghana, for Africa and for communities in the diaspora who share in our aspirations,” he said. He added: “This recognition belongs to every customer who trusts us and every staff member who makes it happen. OmniBSIC Bank is not just another bank, and moments like this remind us exactly why.” In 2026, he has been named Banking CEO of the Year (Africa) and Banking CEO of the Year (Ghana), adding to his 2023 Personality of the Year (Private Sector) honour.

items.title: Abuakwa South MP raises concerns over Ghana’s Ebola preparedness after Nigeria case
items.description: A Member of Parliament (MP) for Abuakwa South Constituency, Dr Kingsley Agyemang, has called on the government to strengthen the country’s public health emergency preparedness following the confirmation of an Ebola virus disease case in Nigeria. In a statement issued on Monday, October 26, 2026, the MP warned that Ghana must not become complacent, despite having no confirmed Ebola case, according to the latest official Ghanaian update cited in the statement. The MP urged the Ministry of Health and the Ghana Health Service to intensify disease surveillance, particularly at land borders, activate regional and district rapid response teams and assess the readiness of designated isolation and treatment facilities. The call follows Nigeria’s reported confirmation of an imported case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola on October 20, 2026. The statement said subsequent genomic analysis found the virus to be closely related to a strain identified in Kenya, although this did not establish direct transmission between the two countries. The MP said Ghana’s extensive travel links, commercial activities and population movements across West Africa made it important for the country to strengthen its defences against potential cross-border transmission. While acknowledging the Ministry of Health’s announcement of intensified surveillance and preparedness measures, including enhanced monitoring at Kotoka International Airport, the MP said the government must demonstrate operational readiness across the health system. “The lessons of previous Ebola outbreaks demonstrate that early detection, effective surveillance and rapid response remain our strongest safeguards against a public health emergency,” the statement said. Calls for funding and protection of health workers The MP also called for adequate supplies of personal protective equipment, diagnostic materials and infection prevention resources to support health facilities in responding to a possible outbreak. The statement emphasised the need to protect frontline healthcare workers through practical training, emergency simulation exercises, laboratory preparedness and clear referral protocols. It further urged the government to release funds promptly to support preparedness measures rather than wait for a confirmed case to expose weaknesses in the country’s response system. The MP said public communication must be timely, transparent and evidence-based to educate Ghanaians on Ebola symptoms, preventive measures and appropriate reporting channels without creating unnecessary panic. The statement also called for stronger collaboration with the World Health Organisation, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention and neighbouring countries to improve information sharing and coordinate responses to potential outbreaks. MP questions government’s commitment to preparedness The MP expressed concern about what was described as insufficient publicly demonstrated progress in addressing issues raised in an earlier statement on March 27, 2026, regarding Ghana’s preparedness for public health emergencies. The MP questioned whether the government was unwilling to invest in preventive measures or had failed to prioritise the necessary resources. The statement called on the Minister for Health to account to Parliament and the public for funds allocated, released and spent on emergency preparedness, as well as provide evidence of improvements made since March. “Public health security must be measured by concrete action, not assurances alone,” the MP said. The MP urged the government to use developments in Nigeria as an opportunity to demonstrate the country’s readiness to manage a potential outbreak, warning against waiting until Ghana records its first case before identifying gaps in its emergency response system. The statement concluded that strengthening preparedness, surveillance and response capacity was essential to protecting public health and preventing a potential emergency from escalating. He said Ghana must intensify monitoring at major points of entry, particularly land borders, to minimise the risk of the virus spreading into the country. In a press statement issued on Monday, October 26, Dr Agyemang, who is also a member of Parliament’s Health Committee, said Ghana’s regional travel networks, commercial activities and population movements created potential pathways for disease transmission. “Early detection, effective surveillance and rapid response remain our strongest safeguards against a public health emergency,” he said. Dr Agyemang acknowledged the Ministry of Health’s announcement of intensified surveillance and preparedness measures, including enhanced monitoring at Kotoka International Airport. However, he stressed that preparedness must go beyond public announcements to demonstrate operational readiness across the health system. He called on the government, through the Ministry of Health and the Ghana Health Service, to activate regional and district rapid response teams, assess the readiness of designated isolation and treatment facilities, and ensure adequate supplies of personal protective equipment and diagnostic materials. He also urged the government to prioritise practical training for frontline healthcare workers, emergency simulation exercises, laboratory preparedness and clear referral protocols. “Adequate financial resources must be released promptly to support these interventions rather than waiting until a confirmed case exposes weaknesses in our preparedness,” he said. The MP further called for timely and evidence-based public communication to educate Ghanaians on Ebola symptoms, preventive measures and appropriate reporting channels without creating unnecessary fear. He also urged stronger collaboration with the World Health Organisation, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention and neighbouring countries to facilitate information sharing and coordinated responses. Dr Agyemang expressed concern about what he described as insufficient publicly demonstrated progress in addressing issues he raised in an earlier statement on March 27, 2026, regarding Ghana’s public health emergency preparedness. He called on the Minister for Health to provide Parliament and the public with a clear account of funds allocated, released and utilised for emergency preparedness, alongside evidence of operational improvements achieved since March. “Public health security must be measured by concrete action, not assurances alone,” he said. Dr Agyemang noted that no Ebola case had been confirmed in Ghana as of the latest official Ghanaian update cited in his statement, but cautioned against complacency. “Ghana must not wait for its first confirmed Ebola case before discovering gaps in its public health emergency response system,” he said. items.title: 3e Sommet Russie-Afrique: le Camarade Premier ministre représente le Président du Faso à Moscou
items.description: Le Camarade Premier ministre, Chef du Gouvernement, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ou é draogo, repr é sentant le Pr é sident du Faso, Chef de l ’É tat, le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim Traor é , a quitt é Ouagadougou ce lundi 26 octobre 2026 pour Moscou, en F é d é ration de Russie. Il prendra part, les 28 et 29 octobre, au troisième Sommet Russie–Afrique et au Forum économique et humanitaire qui l’accompagne. ‎Après les éditions de Sotchi en 2019 et de Saint-Pétersbourg en 2023, cette rencontre réunira les dirigeants africains autour du Président russe Vladimir POUTINE pour donner une nouvelle impulsion au partenariat russo-africain. Elle permettra de dresser le bilan du plan d’action 2023-2026 et de définir les prochaines orientations de la coopération. L’adoption d’une déclaration et d’un nouveau plan d’action pour la période 2027-2029 est prévue à l’issue des travaux. ‎Les échanges porteront notamment sur le commerce, les investissements, la sécurité alimentaire et énergétique, ainsi que sur la souveraineté des États. Le Forum économique et humanitaire abordera également le développement industriel, les transferts de technologies, la transformation numérique, l’intelligence artificielle et les usages pacifiques de l’énergie nucléaire, ainsi que la santé, l’éducation et la formation. ‎À la tête de la délégation burkinabè, le Chef du Gouvernement portera, au nom du Camarade Président du Faso, les priorités nationales, avec pour objectif de promouvoir des projets concrets en matière de transformation locale des ressources, de maîtrise des technologies et de formation de la jeunesse. Ces perspectives de coopération visent à renforcer les capacités productives du pays et à consolider sa souveraineté économique. ‎En marge des travaux, le Premier ministre aura des entretiens bilatéraux et accordera des audiences pour approfondir les partenariats au service de la sécurité et du développement du Burkina Faso. ‎Cette participation s’inscrit dans la dynamique de renforcement des relations entre Ouagadougou et Moscou, confortée par la signature, le 12 février 2026, de l’Accord sur les fondements des relations entre les deux pays. Elle traduit la volonté du Président du Faso de diversifier les partenariats, dans le respect de la souveraineté nationale, de l’égalité et des intérêts réciproques, afin d’apporter des réponses concrètes aux défis sécuritaires, humanitaires et de développement du Burkina Faso. ‎ DCRP/Primature L’article 3e Sommet Russie-Afrique: le Camarade Premier ministre représente le Président du Faso à Moscou est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: New Rural Service Centre to advance climate-resilient cocoa farming in Ahafo Region
items.description: …Proforest facility in Asumura will extend practical services for farmers and strengthen sustainable land-use governance Proforest has commissioned a new Rural Service Centre in Asumura, Asunafo North Municipality in the Ahafo Region, to expand support for cocoa farmers seeking to improve productivity, strengthen climate resilience and protect forests. Established under the Building Deforestation-free Climate Resilient Cocoa Landscape programme with funding support from the Walmart Foundation, the Centre will provide technical training, farm-management services and a local platform for community leadership and social and environmental governance. The Asumura facility builds on Proforest’s first Rural Service Centre, commissioned at Dadiesoaba in the Asutifi South District in 2024. That Centre now provides technical training and farm-management services for farmers and surrounding communities. Hon. Joseph Akparibo, Municipal Chief Executive of Asunafo North, said: “This project being carried out within the framework of the Ghana Cocoa Forest REDD+ Programme (GCFRP), is closely aligned with the Government’s Agriculture for Economic Transformation Agenda and its flagship Feed Ghana Programme. Feed Ghana seeks to raise productivity, strengthen food security, create jobs, supply raw materials to industry and connect farmers to markets.” Abraham Baffoe, Executive Director, Global and Africa, Proforest, said: “Through our collective efforts, we are demonstrating that sustainable production, environmental stewardship, and community development can go hand in hand. Let us continue to demonstrate that together, we can build a prosperous, climate-resilient, and deforestation-free landscape for current and future generations.” Walmart Foundation, the funder of this project emphasised the importance of collaboration. “We are very proud to support this work and look forward to seeing how farmers use it to help grow more sustainable cocoa and how the community uses it to help advance local governance of the landscape initiative”, said Simon Hall, Director of Strategic Initiatives at Walmart Foundation. The Asumura Rural Service Centre marks an important step in strengthening climate-resilient and deforestation-free cocoa production in the Ahafo Region. By bringing technical training, farm-management support and community-led governance closer to farmers, the facility will help improve livelihoods and productivity while promoting responsible land use and forest protection. It also demonstrates the value of collaboration among communities, government, development partners and the private sector in building a more sustainable and resilient cocoa landscape for present and future generations. items.title: A Map for Loving America
items.description: S tevie Wonder’s outfit seemed, at first, to be a strange choice. It was September 1976, and the 26-year-old Grammy winner, better known at that point for appearing on his album covers with a short afro or in cornrows and a tunic, was wearing a cowboy outfit: a collared, cream-colored shirt and matching trousers, a terra-cotta bandanna around his neck, a wide-brimmed hat. He also had a double holster wrapped around his hips, reading: NUMBER ONE WITH A BULLET . Maureen Orth, then a young writer for Newsweek , was confused. Along with a herd of other journalists, she had traveled to a 145-acre farm in North Brookfield, Massachusetts, for a listening party for Songs in the Key of Life —Wonder’s new, 17-track album, which he was releasing along with a four-track EP, for a grand total of 105 minutes of soul-stirring sound. Western iconography hadn’t been on the menu, or so she thought. “It’s like, what? Stevie, you’re a cowboy? Why?” Orth recalled on the 2024 podcast The Wonder of Stevie , which I co-created and co-produced. (Wonder executive-produced.) “We haven’t heard the songs yet, but there aren’t any cowboy songs on the record.” Orth was right: Nothing on the album sounded remotely like a cowboy song. But Wonder’s getup wasn’t so much about communicating the content of his opus as it was about playfully claiming the context around it. And that context was that he, a uniquely brilliant symbol of American promise, had sought and captured something uniquely, brilliantly American. Five decades later, Songs ’ message—one of optimism, resolve, and self-belief in the shadow of hyper-partisan politics and communities coming apart—still feels urgent. Which makes it seem right that Wonder recently began a 17-city tour across Europe and the United States to mark the 50th anniversary of the record’s release, putting on shows in which he is playing the entire album. A lot was going on in the country back when Songs came out. It was the United States’ bicentennial, and although the nation had reason to celebrate, people also had much to mourn: race riots, economic recession, repeated paroxysms from the corrupt presidency of Richard Nixon. At the time, Wonder had been experiencing a sadness and disillusionment about politics and U.S. foreign policy so profound that he had seriously considered leaving the music business and moving to Ghana, where he planned to work with disabled children. “You can sing about things and talk about things,” he had said earlier in the ’70s, “but if your actions don’t speak louder than your words, you’re nothing.” Wonder had gone so far as to announce a “farewell” tour. (Some believed this was a tactic to get a better deal as he renegotiated his contract with his label, Tamla, a division of Motown Records.) When Songs arrived, then, it seemed to be a reassertion of his primacy within American popular culture—and perhaps of his belief in America itself. Time magazine reported that the album took Wonder more than two years to produce. It cooked for so long that Motown executives had T-shirts made featuring a play on the phrase that Wonder kept using when asked about the project’s status: WE’RE ALMOST FINISHED . What they didn’t know was that Wonder, rather than struggling, was perfecting the simple message at the album’s heart—that to express love for America requires not only celebrating it with fireworks and flags but also acknowledging its missteps and failings. S ongs is a deeply personal album for millions of people. (The singer-songwriter India.Arie, born in 1975, has described it as a record that “feels like family.”) In fact, I’d initially thought of starting this article by describing how the record was the primary soundtrack to my early life—from the weekend afternoons of my childhood, when I studied the album’s liner notes and lyrics as my dad’s turntable crackled in the background, to one particularly tumultuous year during my 20s, when, rocked by a breakup, I shut myself in my bedroom, slid a disc into my CD player, and sang along to “I Wish,” “Joy Inside My Tears,” and “As.” Over the years, I came to realize that the album owes much of its enduring power to its relevance as a source of personal and political optimism. It is a love letter to the listener but also a message, marked urgent , to a nation. When I say that Songs in the Key of Life —consistently voted one of the best albums of all time—is uniquely American, I mean that it is both by America and of it. At that farm in 1976, Wonder’s outfit was a clever play on his argument about his country, but his songs provided the substance. They spoke of love and hope and faith and history and family and even fear. The first track, “Love’s in Need of Love Today,” offered a quiet opener with a devastating message: The country was veering from its imagined ideal. Hate was “goin’ ’round,” Wonder sang, “Breaking many hearts / Stop it please / Before it’s gone too far.” The album’s third song, “Village Ghetto Land,” was where things started to get real. It was a nearly three-and-a-half-minute indictment of the economic and geographical segregation visited on America’s less fortunate, set to sober, almost mournful electronic strings. From there, the record unfolded like a map of the United States’ psyche, the soundtrack of a people (well, some people) who were wrestling with the gap between the stated promise of this country and its sobering reality. Its eighth song, “Pastime Paradise”—which later inspired the 1995 Coolio hit “Gangsta’s Paradise”—was about coming to terms with an idealized past that had never actually existed. The lyrics chide people who glorify times “long gone behind,” those “wasting most their days / In remembrance of ignorance oldest praise.” Wonder cautions those living with a romanticized view of history against succumbing to inertia. He invites those whose nostalgia blinds them to the present to confront the truth of the past, to move toward a brighter future. “Tell me, who of them will come to be?” he sang. “How many of them are you and me?” Then there was “Black Man,” perhaps the album’s most explicitly political track: a head-thumping, funk-inflected assertion about people of color’s contributions to the creation of America. Name-dropping figures including Squanto and Sacagawea, Benjamin Banneker and Harriet Tubman, Wonder sang: We pledge allegiance All our lives To the magic colors Red, blue, and white But we all must be given The liberty that we defend For with justice not for all men History will repeat again It’s time we learned This world was made for all men F or years, rumors circulated that Wonder had considered dozens or even more than 100 songs for inclusion on the record, many of which people never would have heard. So it was a delight when, on the date of the album’s anniversary this year, September 28, he surprised the music world by releasing on streaming services Songs in the Key of Life—The EP , a quartet of previously unreleased tracks from the era when he was recording the original album. I was excited at first. But after listening to the EP a few times, I felt uninspired. I wanted more than what I’d heard (lyrics mostly about love, loss, and regret). So, I reached out to the cultural critic Wesley Morris, a Stevie stan like I am, and the host of The Wonder of Stevie. I wrote to him that one of the “new” songs (“It’s Easier”) felt a little stale, reminiscent of Wonder’s 1971 work Where I’m Coming From . “I’m Into Livin’” felt very Hotter Than July , the album that Wonder released four years after Songs in the Key of Life . And the others seemed like sentimental-bordering-on-empty attempts at saying something that—well, I couldn’t quite figure it out. To be clear, I was in a horrible mood. The promise of America that Wonder had celebrated in Songs has been feeling, to me, further away than ever. The Trump administration has been unraveling many of the rights that previous generations worked so hard and long to ensure. It has been unleashing violent law enforcement in cities across the country; instigating political witch hunts ; trying to make it harder to vote ; and, contra “Black Man,” attempting to control how our national history is told, in part by downplaying the role that women and people of color have played in the political and cultural project that is America. I was also frustrated. All this strife, all the ways in which the world has gone backwards, and Wonder had released four new songs about love? Then I remembered something that Morris had said on The Wonder of Stevie : “Anytime you hear a Black American singing about love, what you’re hearing is a choice not to be singing about a dozen other things. Being poor, getting ripped off, going to court or prison, driving your brother or your cousin to court, visiting them in prison. Talking about how affirmative action doesn’t need to end. Talking about voting rights and why that’s important.” When these are the realities people are facing, a song about love—romance, love of people, love of community—can become its own declaration of independence. “In its own quiet way,” Morris said on the podcast, “a Black love song says, Here. Here’s my heart . And despite all of this other shit—betrayal, neglect, struggle, rage, lunacy, the pernicious old status quo,” he added, Wonder is asking: “ Would you look at the world? How is it that I can know all of this and still make this gorgeous, contiguously gorgeous sound that is this whole album? This is the story of us all .” That story evolves in fits and starts, and circles back on itself before moving forward—in a pattern somewhat similar to the cover art for Songs in the Key of Life , which to me evokes a spiral of warm, heavenly clouds. Wonder, a modern griot, understands that people need to tell stories to make sense of a complicated world, and that they need to believe in those stories to keep faith. As he sings in “Sir Duke,” the album’s fifth song and an homage to great American songwriters and singers such as Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Louis Armstrong, and Ella Fitzgerald, “Music is a world within itself.” With Songs , Wonder created a soundtrack, too, a picture of the world as it was—and of what it could become.

items.title: The Collapse of Cuba
items.description: Photographs by Moises Saman A priest led me up battered stairs to a tiny room at the top of a church. From the window, we gazed down at the decayed colonial villas and scattered trash fires of eastern Havana. He pointed to the yellow wall behind us, where someone had sketched a meticulous map of the local street grid. “They posted armed guards here, to watch over us,” he said. Cuba’s Communist government, the priest said, took over the convent, cloister, and school of Los Escolapios after the revolution of 1959, expelling the nuns and setting up a guard post—one part of the regime’s sprawling apparatus of surveillance and control. The church downstairs was virtually closed, the congregation mostly exiled or jailed in accordance with Communist Cuba’s atheist principles. The guards are gone now, along with the portraits of Fidel Castro and the secular schoolteachers who commandeered the convent’s lower floors after the revolution. The church is in the process of reclaiming the magnificent 18th-century cloister from the state, which left it in ruins. The priest, Iván Guerra Álvarez, made clear he believes that history is approaching another turning point, and that the Communist regime will soon be gone. “The Church will play a big role in the transition,” he told me. “We are the biggest institution in Cuba outside the government.” No one can say when or how that transition will happen. Donald Trump may or may not have “the honor of taking Cuba,” as he boasted after imposing an oil blockade on the island earlier this year. The Cuban regime has stifled any viable domestic opposition. But the withering of the state—a process that has been under way for decades—has accelerated, and is shocking to see up close. The ration cards that used to guarantee basic foodstuffs for every Cuban had been blank for weeks when I visited in August. Police and soldiers were once ubiquitous throughout the country, but I saw hardly any. In far-eastern Cuba, I met a fisherman who told me that he and others like him, who lacked electricity for refrigeration, have gone back to traditional methods of drying and salting fish. The average monthly salary for public-sector employees in Cuba—including doctors and teachers—is about 6,500 pesos, which is less than $10 and far below the cost of a subsistence diet (a single carton of eggs can cost up to 4,700 pesos). Even getting small amounts of cash can be a trial: Banks sometimes limit withdrawals to 1,000 pesos (less than $1.50) per person per day. Moises Saman for The Atlantic A former boarding school in Cienfuegos, established after the 1959 Revolution, where students combined classroom education with agricultural labor The government still purports—on faded billboards, in party speeches—to meet all of the material and spiritual needs of its citizens, but it is now bankrupt in every sense . Almost no one believes in the system anymore, and many, especially outside Havana, behave as if the government simply does not exist. As in the Soviet-dominated Eastern bloc during its final years, destitution is leading people back to older faiths. Afro Cuban Santeria and Catholicism have flourished, and “house churches” have proliferated, often evangelical and sometimes consisting of nothing more than a dozen folding chairs in someone’s living room. Guerra Álvarez led me down from the church tower to the main sanctuary of Los Escolapios, an atmospheric shift he half-jokingly likened to a trip from North to South Korea. We found ourselves in a noisy crowd of more than 100 schoolchildren and worshippers. A teacher dressed as an angel, with a white beard, wig, and gown, was giving Bible lessons in the dimly lit nave. Afterward, volunteers handed out lunches of rice and beans. To see so many people looking so cheerful was striking; Cuba is now a country full of empty streets and abandoned buildings, having lost as much as a quarter of its population to migration in the past few years. The expanded role of the churches is partly an outcome of American policy: The U.S. government has long favored the Catholic Church as an intermediary. When the Trump administration approved a $100 million aid package for Cuba in May, it was on the condition that the funds be distributed by faith-based groups and humanitarian organizations. But the rise of religion in Cuba is also a measure of the state’s withdrawal—and perhaps a hint at the island’s future direction. Moises Saman for The Atlantic Teens receive bread and drinks at a Catholic church in Havana. I came to Cuba expecting to see suffering. What I did not anticipate was the near-total collapse of the state. This was evident even in Havana, where all-day blackouts are routine, but things are much worse in the eastern half of the island, which has long been poorer and less developed. Cuba’s religious revival has burned brightest there, especially among Pentecostal churches, whose traditions include faith healing and miracles. [ The David Frum show: Cuba is collapsing. Will Trump invade? ] I drove to the east with the photographer Moises Saman, an 18-hour journey that sometimes made us feel as if we were traveling back in time. Weaving slowly among enormous potholes, we passed few other cars. As we got closer to Santiago de Cuba, Cuba’s second-largest city, we saw almost as many horse-drawn carts as motorized vehicles. Moises Saman for The Atlantic A weathered roadside billboard, bearing a portrait of Fidel Castro, reads, “ Son las ideas las que nos hacen un pueblo combatiente ” (“It is ideas that make us a fighting people). Poverty is not new in the country, but the number of street beggars I saw shocked me. On the seafront in Santiago, a mother and daughter approached me, both of them skeletally thin, to ask for money. The mother, a white-haired 76-year-old, told me that their only means of support had been her son, who had worked as a security guard and died of cancer last year. Now they spend all day begging and collecting plastic bottles in the hopes of trading them for a few pesos, she said. They get nothing from the state. Later, I visited their home, a filthy ground-floor room where they sleep on metal bed frames topped with cardboard instead of mattresses. When I asked whether there was any electricity, the mother said that they did not even have a bulb. Moises Saman for The Atlantic The collapse of the state has left impoverished Cubans with few options besides begging or relying on charity. The failure of Cuba’s health-care system may be the most damning indictment of its Communist regime. Castro once held up the country’s network of local clinics as a model for the world, visible proof that socialism could triumph where capitalism had failed. He sent hundreds of thousands of doctors overseas, an “army of white coats” to bolster Cuba’s image and generate money for the state. (It later emerged that the doctors had been given little choice and many were victims of what has been called forced labor.) Some doctors are still being sent abroad, but more have simply fled Cuba. On Cayo Granma, an island at the entrance to the bay of Santiago, I found a single nurse caring not only for all 870 residents but also for many people from the neighboring coastal areas. She no longer knows how many people she is responsible for, because doctors have been leaving the region so fast that she cannot keep track of the patients forced to seek new care. Her name is Clara Luaces, a woman of 55 with a direct gaze and an air of brisk competence. Her clinic was a room the size of a large closet, hot and crowded with patients when I arrived; outside, it was almost 100 degrees. A 12-year-old boy with a fever sat on a bench, an IV drip in his arm; a girl with a skin infection sat nearby with her mother. “We have to work miracles here,” Luaces said, answering my questions as she checked the boy’s pulse and adjusted his IV. The government had stopped piping water to the island three months earlier, she said, and the resulting lack of clean water had led to a sharp rise in bacterial fevers and skin infections. “Even young people are dying on me,” she said. She was chronically short on medicine and had very little money of her own to supplement the clinic’s supply. The boy began moaning, and Luaces comforted him, putting a pillow under his head and calling him “sweetheart.” “I’m not going to retire,” she said, looking up at me, “because there is no one else to take this on.” Luaces did not want to talk about politics. She confined herself to saying that she had been a student during what Castro dubbed the “special period” in the 1990s, when Cuba went through a severe economic crisis after losing its Soviet patron and the regime seemed on the brink of collapse. What is happening now, she said, is “much more special.” Moises Saman for The Atlantic Two people sit outside a house during a nighttime power outage in Camagüey. Others lashed out directly at the state. Not long ago, the country bristled with informants working for the Committees for the Defense of the Revolution. But when I asked people about the CDR, some laughed, and few seemed worried about being overheard. One evening on a beach in Baracoa, a man in his 30s asked me what I thought about Communism. He was lying in a hammock talking with four other men, drinking cheap sugarcane rum from a plastic bottle; they had been complaining about the ever higher prices of rice, beans, and other basic foods. I told him I thought Communism was a lousy way to run a country. He looked squarely at me and said, “I shit on Fidel Castro’s mother.” The other men laughed. He uttered a few more obscenities. Then, suddenly, all of the humor drained from the man’s face. His voice went taut with anger, and tears welled up in his eyes. “Cuba is frozen in time!” he shouted. “There’s no hope. It’s a sad thing to be born a Cuban. That’s what I think, and I don’t care; they can send me to prison if they want.” The other men had gone silent. Here is another measure of Cubans’ anger at their government: During nine days of travel around the island, I did not meet a single person who blamed Donald Trump or the United States for their situation. I sometimes reminded them about the blockade Trump had started earlier this year , cutting Cubans off from the cheap oil that Venezuela had been supplying before the U.S. military captured Nicolás Maduro in January. Hadn’t things gotten worse since then? [ Read: Cuba’s old economic model is ‘exhausted’ ] “I don’t see any change since January,” a retired engineer named Guillermo Almeida told me. “That oil from Venezuela wasn’t reaching the people anyway.” He and others said that the more important turning point was the coronavirus pandemic, which destroyed Cuba’s tourism industry and shrank the value of remittances from family members abroad that many Cubans depend on, exposing more fully a state that had long been depleted. Another man put it differently: “It seems to us that the real embargo is inside of Cuba.” The churches have taken on much of the Cuban state’s old role in keeping people alive. In Baracoa, I met Raul de Jesus Muñoz Munder, a Pentecostal pastor who has been evangelizing in the area for 32 years. He had seen hunger and deprivation, he said, including during the years he spent in a tiny church in the mountains, but nothing as bad as the present. Muñoz Munder described his work almost as if it were a military operation. Every week, he said, he meets with a team of associate pastors at his church, and each man reports on the situation in his home neighborhood: who is sick and needs medicine, who needs food, and how to get it to them. The pastor’s congregation has about 1,100 regular members, but he provides aid to a much larger group. His denomination, the Assemblies of God, has expanded from two to 40 churches in the Baracoa region over the past three decades. The growth of the evangelical movement is hard to quantify in Cuba, where the Catholic Church was once almost universal. No independent numbers on religious affiliation exist—the government has long had a lock on surveys. But everyone I spoke with, both inside and outside the country, agreed that the evangelical presence has surged in recent years. Moises Saman for The Atlantic The pastor and a church secretary at the Iglesia Evangélica Pentecostal Asambleas de Dios de Baracoa, in Baracoa, in eastern Cuba. The congregation is one of the city’s most active Protestant churches. In Baracoa, I stumbled upon several different evangelical services one Saturday evening, each of them loud and raucous, the congregation on its feet and clapping along. These kinds of scenes are still a little jarring to many older Cubans. They tend to associate church with more orderly Catholic rituals, and grew up without seeing much of the flamboyant evangelical religiosity that has become common across Latin America. But the island is changing. I heard a fair amount of God talk even on the street. One afternoon in Camagüey, a beautiful, decaying city in east-central Cuba, an elderly woman in a wheelchair called out to me as I passed her open front door. “We have to tell people that God exists,” she said, in an urgent tone. “God’s word has to be fulfilled in its entirety.” One of her children had left the country, and the other one, a high-school teacher, was in prison; she said he’d been given a 14-year sentence for accusing a high-ranking official of corruption. The old woman was living alone, and the only thing she had left was her faith. In Havana, I visited a nursing home owned by the Catholic Church that was full of former civil servants and military officers. In one room I found a dozen old men, their beds lined up about a yard apart. Each had a single narrow locker for all of his earthly possessions. A nurse gave me permission to speak with residents but cautioned me that they were “very sad.” Many of them, she explained, had had distinguished government careers but had found themselves abandoned by both the state and their family at the end of their life. In many cases, their children had left the country. Moises Saman for The Atlantic People in need receive a meal at the Concatedral de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, a Catholic cathedral in Baracoa. One of the men, a wiry 65-year-old, had fought for two years in Angola, where Castro had sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers in the 1970s and ’80s to support a Communist-aligned government. The former soldier had once been a fan of the revolution; you could tell because he had a big tattoo of Che Guevara on his right arm. He’d gotten it when he was 18. He showed me several scars left over from battles in Africa, and I asked him how he felt about the situation in the country. [ From the September 1964 issue: An eyewitness account of Cuba’s fumbling Marxism ] He answered with an expletive. I asked him what should be done to make things better. Cuba needed to be bombed, he told me. Specifically, Raúl Castro, Fidel’s brother and successor, should be bombed. And Raúl’s daughter Mariela. And the prime minister, Manuel Marrero Cruz. Again and again during my travels on the island, people told me: Cuba is not like this . They didn’t just mean the hunger and sickness and lack of electricity. They meant the anger, the emptiness, the absence of music and laughter. There used to be a musical group on every corner of Santiago, an 81-year-old man who had spent 45 years as a singer in a band recalled. Now there were none. After the 1959 revolution, Fidel Castro enshrined atheism in the new state, exiling many prominent Catholic figures and sending believers to reeducation camps. But in a sense, he did not so much banish religion as create a new cult, with its own rituals and holy martyrs. That cult staggers on today in a weird half life, abandoned by most of its people after decades of misery and repression, yet somehow defying a final collapse. Moises Saman for The Atlantic Soldiers perform a changing-of-the-guard ceremony at Santa Ifigenia Cemetery in Santiago, where Fidel Castro’s remains are entombed. The only immaculately clean place I saw in all of Cuba was the Santa Ifigenia Cemetery, where Fidel’s ashes are held, in Santiago. The grass there is green and mowed to razor-perfection, the walkways carefully swept; not a single visitor was in sight when I went there. As I stood looking at the rounded granite boulder that marks Fidel’s tomb, patriotic music began blaring from invisible loudspeakers, and an honor guard of soldiers in neatly pressed uniforms began goose-stepping in unison, rifles pointed skyward. They marched to the mausoleum honoring José Martí, Cuba’s great nationalist hero; presented arms; and relieved a group of similarly uniformed compatriots, who marched back. They do this changing of the guard every half hour, all day long, I was told. Watching those perfect soldiers, you could believe for a moment that you were in another place—perhaps that far-off country Castro had dreamed of, where socialism is triumphant, no one is sick or unhappy, and everyone aspires to follow the heroic example of the man who led a glorious revolution. Then a breeze swept across the grass, carrying the acrid stench of burning garbage, and I remembered where I was. This article appears in the December 2026 print edition with the headline “How Castro’s Cuba Ends.”

items.title: Moustapha Guirassy : « Il ne faut pas coincer le Sénégal dans une logique trop technocratique, c’est un danger »
items.description: Prenant part, ce dimanche 25 octobre 2026, à la conférence de presse du gouvernement, le ministre de l’Éducation nationale, Moustapha Guirassy, a appelé les députés de Pastef-Les Patriotes à faire preuve de responsabilité, avant de les inviter à voter, mardi prochain, le projet de loi de finances rectificative (Lfr) 2026. « Enfermer la volonté des Sénégalais dans la coquille simplement d’un parti, ce serait rompre, en fait, avec les Sénégalais. Il ne faut pas coincer le Sénégal dans une logique trop technocratique, c’est un danger. Ce moment appelle un effort de tous pour comprendre ce qui se passe. Il y a la puissance, mais il y a une miséricorde et la capacité de pardonner. J’en appelle à la spiritualité parce que ce qui est en train de se jouer est critique », a déclaré le ministre. Par ailleurs, Moustapha Guirassy a rappelé l’effort consenti dans le recrutement de 8.000 enseignants entre 2024 et 2026. Selon lui, malgré des conditions très difficiles, l’effort dans le secteur social de l’éducation nationale se poursuit, notamment à travers les recrutements et la formation. « Alors qu’en 2023, il n’y avait que 800 personnes formées, ce chiffre a été multiplié par 113 dans les structures de formation, ce qui est du jamais vu. Malgré la situation difficile, 2.500 salles de classe ont été réalisées à l’élémentaire, démontrant que l’engagement de l’État est bien là », a-t-il fait savoir. Le ministre a également indiqué qu’un projet de création d’un Fonds autonome pour le financement de l’éducation était sur la table du président de la République. Une initiative qui, selon lui, va complètement changer la donne. « L’Éducation nationale est dans un processus de refondation avec des investissements massifs. Bien que les demandes soient pressantes, un sursaut est nécessaire pour franchir ce cap », a-t-il conclu. A. DIOUF
